questions.stem: What is a primary source in history?
options: A source created at the time being studied
A modern historian's book about the period
A textbook summary
A documentary made recently
questions.explanation: Letters, tools and inscriptions from the period are primary. Later accounts are secondary.

questions.stem: What is a secondary source?
options: An eyewitness statement
An account created later that interprets primary sources
An object made during the period studied
A photograph taken at the time
questions.explanation: A historian's analysis is secondary, however well researched.
questions.teaching:
Sources are classified by their relationship in time to the events they describe, and that is the only test.

Anything created at the time by someone involved or present is primary — letters, diaries, photographs, film footage, objects, official records made on the day. Anything produced afterwards, interpreting and drawing on those, is the other category: a textbook, a documentary, a historian's article. This question has one option standing apart from three that group together, which is worth noticing. Neither type is more reliable in general; each has to be judged on who made it and why.

questions.stem: What does an archaeologist study?
options: Only fossils of animals
Physical remains such as artefacts, buildings and burials
Only written records
Only living cultures
questions.explanation: Archaeology recovers material evidence, which is essential for societies with few or no written records.

questions.stem: What is an artefact?
options: An object made or used by people in the past
A natural rock formation
A written law
A modern replica
questions.explanation: Artefacts are human-made, which is what makes them evidence of human activity.
questions.teaching:
Historians work from evidence, and the physical evidence has its own vocabulary.

Objects made, shaped or used by people in the past are one category — tools, pottery, coins, weapons, jewellery, clothing. Archaeologists recover them, and they are especially valuable for periods with no writing, since they are the only record left. A written source is different, and a natural object with no human involvement is different again. The test is whether a person made or used it.

questions.stem: What does BCE stand for?
options: Before Common Era
Before Chronological Era
British Common Era
Before Calendar Establishment
questions.explanation: BCE and CE are the non-religious equivalents of BC and AD.
questions.teaching:
Dating conventions changed to make them usable across cultures, and the newer labels sit alongside the older ones.

The traditional pair was tied to a specific religious event. The newer pair keeps exactly the same numbering but renames the eras so they do not assume a particular faith — one for years counted forward from the reference point, one for years counted back from it. So the numbers are unchanged and only the labels differ, which means the two systems can be converted with no arithmetic at all.

questions.stem: Which came first, 500 BCE or 200 BCE?
options: 500 BCE
200 BCE
They are the same year
It cannot be determined
questions.explanation: BCE years count backwards, so a larger number is earlier.
questions.teaching:
Dating systems run in two directions from a common point, and one of them counts backwards.

Dates after that point count upwards, so a larger number is more recent. Dates before it count downwards towards it, so a larger number is *further* back in time. That reversal catches almost everyone at first. When ordering dates on that side, the bigger figure is the earlier event — and when a timeline crosses the boundary, both systems appear on the same line running left to right.

questions.stem: What is chronology?
options: A type of primary source
The arrangement of events in time order
The study of ancient languages
The study of artefacts
questions.explanation: Chronology is the backbone of historical reasoning — you cannot argue cause and effect without it.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'continuity' in history?
options: Aspects of life that stay the same over time
Events that change quickly
The order of events
A type of source
questions.explanation: Continuity and change are studied together: what persisted and what altered.

questions.stem: What does 'civilisation' generally refer to?
options: A complex society with cities, organised government and specialised roles
Any group of people living together
A society with no agriculture
A single family group
questions.explanation: The usual markers are urban settlement, social hierarchy, specialisation and often writing.

questions.stem: What development allowed early societies to build permanent settlements?
options: The building of pyramids
The use of iron tools
Agriculture, which provided a reliable food supply
The invention of writing
questions.explanation: A dependable surplus made staying in one place viable, which then enabled specialisation.

questions.stem: Roughly how long have Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples lived in Australia?
options: At least 65 000 years
About 2 000 years
About 10 000 years
About 500 years
questions.explanation: Archaeological evidence from sites such as Madjedbebe supports occupation of at least 65 000 years, making these the world's oldest continuing cultures.

questions.stem: What is 'Country' in the context of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures?
options: A term for the lands, waters and skies a group belongs to, including cultural connection
A defined territory with recognised borders, held by a group under Australian property law
The area a group moved through seasonally, mapped by the routes taken rather than by ownership
A region named by early surveyors after the group they recorded as living there at the time
questions.explanation: Country carries meanings of belonging, responsibility and identity, well beyond a simple area of land.

questions.stem: What are oral traditions?
options: Knowledge and accounts passed down by spoken word across generations
Written records kept in archives
Objects buried at a site
Modern historians' interpretations
questions.explanation: Oral traditions are a form of historical evidence, and some Aboriginal accounts preserve information about events thousands of years old.

questions.stem: What is a hypothesis in a historical investigation?
options: A primary source
A date on a timeline
A proposed explanation to be tested against evidence
A proven conclusion
questions.explanation: Historians propose explanations and then test them against the surviving evidence.

questions.stem: Which of these is a primary source for studying ancient Rome?
options: A recent museum guidebook
A Roman coin minted at the time
A modern film about Rome
A school textbook
questions.explanation: The coin was made in the period. Everything else interprets it later.

questions.stem: What is a significant individual in history?
options: A person mentioned in one source
A person whose actions had a substantial effect on their society
The most famous person alive today
Any person who lived in the past
questions.explanation: Significance is judged by impact and consequence, not fame alone.

questions.stem: What was one important feature of many early societies?
options: Shared religious beliefs that varied little between settlements
The development of trade with other groups
A social structure in which every member held equal status
Technology limited to tools that needed no specialist knowledge
questions.explanation: Trade, technology, social groups, laws and beliefs are the features the curriculum names.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'perspective' in history?
options: The physical location of a site
The number of sources available
The point of view of a person or group, shaped by their circumstances
The date an event happened
questions.explanation: Different people experienced the same event differently, which is why multiple sources matter.

questions.stem: What is a legacy in history?
options: A written will
An artefact found at a site
The date something ended
The lasting effects of a person, event or society on later times
questions.explanation: Roman roads and legal ideas are legacies that outlasted the empire.

questions.stem: Why is archaeology especially important for studying societies without writing?
options: Those societies were less complex
Written records exist for every society
Archaeology can determine exact thoughts
Physical remains are the main surviving evidence of how people lived
questions.explanation: Material evidence carries the weight when there is no text to read.

questions.stem: Why do historians use more than one source when investigating an event?
options: It makes the investigation longer
Sources must always agree
Each source has limits and bias, so comparing them gives a fuller picture
One source is never accurate
questions.explanation: Corroboration and contradiction between sources is how reliability is tested.

questions.stem: How did the physical environment influence the development of ancient Egypt?
options: Egypt relied entirely on rainfall
The Nile's predictable flooding supported agriculture and settlement along its banks
The desert provided rich farmland
The environment had no influence
questions.explanation: The annual inundation deposited fertile silt, which is why settlement concentrated along a narrow strip.

questions.stem: What can burial sites tell historians about a society?
options: Nothing reliable
The exact language spoken
Beliefs about death, social status and available technology
Only the age of the person buried
questions.explanation: Grave goods and burial style reveal beliefs and hierarchy — richer burials usually indicate social stratification.

questions.stem: Why is 'continuity and change' a useful pair of concepts?
options: It prevents assuming everything changed, or that nothing did, over a period
It only applies to modern history
Change is the only thing worth studying
It replaces the need for evidence
questions.explanation: Periods of dramatic change usually contain much that stayed the same, and vice versa.

questions.stem: What does the archaeological evidence at Australian sites such as Madjedbebe demonstrate?
options: A very long and continuous human occupation of the continent
That occupation began but was later interrupted
That occupation was seasonal rather than continuous
That the earliest sites are all coastal
questions.explanation: Dating of artefacts at such sites has repeatedly pushed occupation dates back, supporting continuity over tens of thousands of years.

questions.stem: How did Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples respond to environmental change during Deep Time?
options: They moved permanently to a single sheltered region
They abandoned the continent
They relied entirely on imported food
They adapted their movement, food sources and land management as conditions changed
questions.explanation: Sea level rise after the last ice age, for example, changed coastlines dramatically, and communities adapted their patterns of use accordingly.

questions.stem: Why should cultural protocols be followed when studying Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories?
options: Communities hold authority over their own cultural knowledge, and some material is restricted
Because researchers must publish before communities do
Because oral accounts cannot be checked against records
Because museums hold the legal rights to the material
questions.explanation: Respecting who may share what knowledge is both an ethical requirement and part of the curriculum.

questions.stem: Why might two historians interpret the same evidence differently?
options: Interpretation is not part of history
They may weigh sources differently or ask different questions of them
One must be dishonest
Evidence has only one possible meaning
questions.explanation: Historical interpretation involves judgement. Debate between interpretations is normal and productive.

questions.stem: Why is the absence of evidence not the same as evidence of absence?
options: All evidence survives
Historians should ignore missing evidence
Materials decay and records are lost, so something may have existed without surviving
Absence of evidence proves nothing existed
questions.explanation: Organic materials rarely survive, so activities leaving no durable trace can be invisible archaeologically.

questions.stem: What makes a historical source reliable rather than simply available?
options: Its closeness to events, the author's purpose and knowledge, and agreement with other evidence
Its age alone
Whether it is written rather than physical
Whether it is easy to read
questions.explanation: Reliability is assessed against several criteria together, not established by any single feature.

questions.stem: Why do historians treat oral traditions as legitimate historical evidence?
options: They are always more accurate than written records
They require no evaluation
They are only useful as stories
They can preserve accurate information over long periods and are testable against other evidence
questions.explanation: Some Aboriginal oral accounts of coastal change align with geological evidence of sea level rise thousands of years ago — a striking case of corroboration.

questions.stem: Why is judging the significance of an event more than deciding if it was interesting?
options: Significance considers how many were affected, how deeply, and for how long
Significance is purely personal opinion
Only recent events are significant
Significance means the event is well documented
questions.explanation: Historians apply criteria — scale, depth, durability and relevance to later developments.

questions.stem: A source contradicts several others. What is the appropriate response?
options: Discard it immediately
Accept it over the others
Ignore all the sources
Investigate why it differs before discarding or accepting it
questions.explanation: An outlier may be mistaken, or may preserve something the others omit. The reason for the difference is itself informative.

questions.stem: Why is it problematic to judge an ancient society only by modern values?
options: Historians should make no judgements
It obscures why people acted as they did within their own context
Ancient societies had no values
Modern values are always wrong
questions.explanation: Understanding context is not the same as approving of it. Both explanation and ethical judgement have a place, but they are different tasks.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to study a range of perspectives on a historical event?
options: It shows which account was recorded closest to the event
It allows the most detailed perspective to be identified
It reveals which groups kept the most complete records
Different groups experienced the event differently, and a single perspective distorts it
questions.explanation: Accounts written by the powerful dominate the record, so seeking other perspectives corrects a systematic imbalance.

questions.stem: What is a century?
options: A period of 50 years
A period of 100 years
A period of 10 years
A period of 1000 years
questions.explanation: A decade is 10 years and a millennium is 1000.
questions.teaching:
Historians use standard blocks of time, and two of them are easy to mix up.

One covers a hundred years, and the numbering is the trap: the years beginning with 19 belong to the twentieth of them, because the first ran from year 1 to year 100. The other block covers ten times as long. A decade covers ten years. Knowing the sizes lets you convert between 'the 1800s' and 'the nineteenth century', which is a conversion history questions ask for constantly.

questions.stem: What is a millennium?
options: A period of 1000 years
A period of 100 years
A period of 10 years
A period of 500 years
questions.explanation: Deep time in Australian history spans many tens of millennia.
questions.teaching:
Time is divided into standard blocks, and each has a name based on a Latin number word.

A decade takes its name from the Latin for ten. A century takes its from the word for a hundred, which also gives us 'cent' and 'percentage'. And the largest of the common blocks takes its name from 'mille', the word for a thousand — the same root as millimetre and millipede. Working from the Latin number tells you the length without memorising each term separately.

questions.stem: What is a timeline used for?
options: Showing events in chronological order
Listing sources
Explaining causes
Comparing perspectives
questions.explanation: Timelines make sequence and duration visible at a glance.
questions.teaching:
Historical thinking depends on sequence, and a timeline is the standard tool for making sequence visible.

It places events along a line in the order they happened, usually with the spacing proportional to the time between them — which shows at a glance where things clustered and where long gaps sat. That makes it useful for spotting which events could possibly have influenced which others, since a cause has to come before its effect. It shows order and duration; it does not by itself show causes.

questions.stem: What is an eyewitness account?
options: An archaeological report
A description by someone who was present at the event
A modern historian's analysis
A summary in a textbook
questions.explanation: Eyewitness accounts are primary but still shaped by perspective and memory.

questions.stem: What is excavation in archaeology?
options: The writing of a report
The careful digging and recording of a site
The dating of an artefact
The display of finds in a museum
questions.explanation: Recording exactly where each object is found is as important as the object itself.

questions.stem: Why is the position of an artefact within a site important?
options: It reveals the material the object was made from
It shows whether the object was imported or made locally
Its depth and surroundings help date it and show how it was used
It identifies which excavation team recovered it
questions.explanation: Context is what turns an object into evidence.

questions.stem: What is a hierarchy in an ancient society?
options: A religious ceremony
A method of farming
A ranking of people by status or power
A form of writing
questions.explanation: Social hierarchy is one of the features that marks a complex society.

questions.stem: What is trade?
options: The building of temples
The exchange of goods or services between groups
The taking of land by force
The writing of laws
questions.explanation: Trade networks spread goods, technology and ideas.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'Deep Time' in an Australian context?
options: The very long period of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander presence and history
The last two hundred years
The time before the Earth formed
A geological era with no people
questions.explanation: Deep Time frames a history measured in tens of thousands of years.

questions.stem: Why might an artefact found near the surface be younger than one found deeper?
options: Surface soil is removed by erosion, exposing older material
Layers usually build up over time, so deeper generally means older
Deeper layers were disturbed by later building work
Objects sink through soil at a steady, known rate
questions.explanation: Stratigraphy relies on this, though disturbance can complicate it.

questions.stem: A source was written 200 years after the event it describes. How should it be treated?
options: As more reliable than eyewitness accounts
As a secondary source whose own sources should be examined
As a primary source
As automatically unreliable
questions.explanation: Later does not mean worthless — but it does mean the chain of evidence matters.

questions.stem: How did the development of agriculture change early societies?
options: It reduced trade as settlements became self-sufficient
It improved diet but left social structures unchanged
It allowed permanent settlement, population growth and specialised roles
It required larger groups to move together seasonally
questions.explanation: A reliable surplus freed some people from food production, enabling specialisation.

questions.stem: Why is it useful to compare sources from different groups within a society?
options: Ordinary people's accounts are usually more reliable
Comparison establishes which account was written first
Rulers and ordinary people experienced events very differently
Different groups recorded events at different times
questions.explanation: The surviving record is skewed towards the powerful and literate, so seeking other voices corrects it.

questions.stem: What does the survival of stone tools but not wooden ones tell us about the evidence?
options: Stone tools were more important
All materials survive equally
The record is biased towards materials that preserve well
Wooden tools were never made
questions.explanation: Preservation bias systematically distorts what archaeology can see.

questions.stem: Why do historians consider the purpose of a source?
options: A source made to persuade or glorify will present events selectively
A source with a clear purpose is more reliable
All sources have the same purpose
Purpose determines the date
questions.explanation: A monument celebrating a victory is designed to impress, not to report neutrally.

questions.stem: How does connection to Country shape Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories?
options: Country is understood differently by each generation
Country carries knowledge, responsibility and identity passed across generations
Country describes the boundaries between language groups
Country refers to the physical features of a region
questions.explanation: Country is central to how history, law and identity are held and transmitted.

questions.stem: Why is 'the oldest continuing cultures' a significant description?
options: It means the cultures have not changed
It refers only to archaeology
It means the cultures are ancient but ended
It reflects unbroken cultural practice over tens of thousands of years
questions.explanation: Continuing is the key word: these are living cultures, not historical remnants.

questions.stem: Why is dating evidence such as radiocarbon important to archaeology?
options: It provides independent estimates of age rather than relying on assumption
It reveals what people believed
It identifies who made an object
It is always exact
questions.explanation: Scientific dating gives an independent check, though every method has a margin of error and limits.

questions.stem: A site yields grain stores, defensive walls and elaborate burials. What can be inferred?
options: A society with no leadership
A purely religious site
An organised society with surplus food, perceived threat and social ranking
A small mobile group
questions.explanation: Combining several kinds of evidence supports a stronger inference than any one alone.

questions.stem: Why is caution needed when applying modern categories to ancient societies?
options: Applying them is acceptable provided the historian states which modern definition they are using
Concepts such as 'nation' or 'religion' may not map onto how those people understood themselves
Written records from the period are too fragmentary to support any general category at all
Modern categories were designed for industrial societies and so only apply from the 1800s onwards
questions.explanation: Imposing modern frameworks can obscure how a society actually functioned.

questions.stem: How can oral tradition and archaeological evidence support each other?
options: Where independent lines of evidence agree, confidence in both increases
Oral tradition replaces archaeology
They can never be compared
Archaeology always overrules oral tradition
questions.explanation: Corroboration across independent sources is a strong form of evidence in any discipline.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of judging an ancient society by its monuments?
options: Monuments tell us everything
Monuments reflect the priorities of elites, not the lives of most people
Monuments are always fake
Monuments cannot be dated
questions.explanation: Grand structures survive and impress, which biases attention towards those who commissioned them.

questions.stem: Why do historians distinguish between a cause and a trigger?
options: Causes always come after triggers
Underlying causes build over time while a trigger sets events in motion
They mean the same thing
Triggers are always more important
questions.explanation: Long-term causes explain why an event was possible; the trigger explains why it happened then.

questions.stem: What is an archaeological site?
options: A library of old books
A place where physical evidence of past human activity is found
Any old building
A museum
questions.explanation: Sites are excavated and recorded carefully to preserve context.

questions.stem: What is a written source?
options: A record in text form, such as a letter or inscription
A tool or artefact
A building
An oral account
questions.explanation: Written sources are one type of evidence among many.

questions.stem: What is a dynasty?
options: A form of writing
A trade route
A succession of rulers from the same family
A type of building
questions.explanation: Egyptian and Chinese history are often organised by dynasty.
questions.teaching:
Rule can pass in different ways, and the vocabulary distinguishes them.

Where power passes down through a single family across generations, that line of rulers has its own name — the Habsburgs in Europe, the Tang and Ming in China, the Tudors in England. The word describes the family line rather than the territory it controls. An empire is territory rather than a bloodline, and a monarchy is a system of rule; a single family can hold all three at once, which is why the terms get tangled.

questions.stem: What is an empire?
options: A religious group
A group of territories ruled by a single authority
A single city
A trading company
questions.explanation: Empires typically expand by conquest and rule diverse peoples.
questions.teaching:
Several words describe political organisation and they are not interchangeable.

A nation is a group sharing identity. A state is a governed territory. A kingdom is ruled by a monarch. And one term describes a collection of territories and peoples, often acquired by conquest, brought under one central authority — usually with the centre taking resources from the rest. Rome, the Mongols, the Ottomans and Britain all fit. The defining feature is one power ruling over other peoples rather than a single homeland.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'significance' in history?
options: How famous someone was
How well documented something is
How recent an event was
How important an event or person was in terms of impact and consequence
questions.explanation: Significance is judged against criteria, not popularity.

questions.stem: What is a historical inquiry?
options: A summary of a textbook
A list of dates
A single opinion
An investigation guided by questions and tested against evidence
questions.explanation: Inquiry begins with a question and proceeds through evidence.

questions.stem: What is meant by an ancient society's 'social structure'?
options: The language they spoke
The food they ate
How people were organised into groups and ranks
The buildings they constructed
questions.explanation: Structure covers roles, status and relationships between groups.

questions.stem: What does 'artefact' distinguish from 'ecofact'?
options: They are the same
Artefacts are natural
Ecofacts are always written
Artefacts are human-made; ecofacts are natural remains such as seeds or bones
questions.explanation: Both are evidence, but of different kinds.

questions.stem: Why is a monument built by a ruler a limited source about ordinary life?
options: It records what the ruler wanted remembered, not daily experience
Monuments are always fake
Monuments cannot be dated
It is a complete record
questions.explanation: Elite sources dominate the surviving record, which skews what we can easily know.

questions.stem: How can climate evidence contribute to historical explanation?
options: Climate determines everything
Climate cannot be reconstructed
Droughts or cooling periods can help explain migration, conflict or collapse
Climate records begin too recently to be useful
questions.explanation: Environmental evidence adds a dimension that written sources often omit.

questions.stem: What can the layout of an ancient city tell historians?
options: Nothing reliable
The language spoken
Priorities such as defence, religion, trade and social division
Only its population
questions.explanation: Walls, temples, marketplaces and housing patterns each reveal priorities.

questions.stem: Why is Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land management increasingly studied by historians and scientists?
options: Practices developed over millennia offer detailed knowledge of Australian environments
It was recorded in detail by early European settlers
It applies mainly to farming rather than fire management
It has been reconstructed from archaeological evidence alone
questions.explanation: Cultural burning and seasonal land use are documented practices with growing recognition.

questions.stem: How can absence in the archaeological record be misinterpreted?
options: Absence shows the site was occupied only briefly
Absence indicates the layer was excavated incorrectly
Absence means the activity happened somewhere nearby instead
Perishable materials leave no trace, so their absence does not prove absence of the activity
questions.explanation: Basketry, textiles and wooden tools rarely survive, yet were widely used.

questions.stem: Why do historians distinguish between short-term and long-term consequences?
options: Immediate effects can differ greatly from what unfolds over generations
Long-term effects are too uncertain to assess
Short-term effects reveal the true cause of an event
Immediate effects are recorded and later ones inferred
questions.explanation: A short-term defeat can produce long-term change, and vice versa.

questions.stem: Which combination of evidence would most strongly support a claim about an ancient society's beliefs?
options: Burial practices, artwork and written or oral accounts pointing in the same direction
A single well-preserved artefact recovered from the most important site
The scale of the buildings that survive, since larger structures imply belief
Accounts by neighbouring peoples describing what they observed from outside
questions.explanation: Multiple independent lines converging is the strongest form of historical argument.

questions.stem: Why is the durability of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander oral traditions historically significant?
options: They record events that written sources of the same period describe in almost identical terms
They were maintained by specialists whose only task was to memorise and repeat them without change
They demonstrate that detailed knowledge can be transmitted accurately across very long periods
They are the earliest spoken records anywhere in the world that have been written down and preserved
questions.explanation: Where accounts align with independently dated geological events, the accuracy of transmission is demonstrable.

questions.stem: During the last ice age, low sea levels joined mainland Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into a single landmass. What is it called?
options: Sahul
Sunda
Gondwana
Wallacea
questions.explanation: Sahul is the name for the ice-age continent made up of Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, joined across what are now Torres Strait and Bass Strait. Sunda was the separate landmass that joined Java, Sumatra and Borneo to mainland Asia. Gondwana is the ancient supercontinent that broke apart tens of millions of years before any humans existed.

questions.stem: Even when ice-age sea levels were at their lowest, people moving from South-East Asia to Sahul still had to cross stretches of open sea. What does this tell historians about the first people to reach Australia?
options: They walked the whole way across a land bridge from Asia
They arrived later, once rising seas made the gaps smaller
They crossed the Pacific Ocean from South America by raft
They built watercraft and could plan sea crossings
questions.explanation: Deep water between the islands of Wallacea never dried out, so reaching Sahul tens of thousands of years ago required boats or rafts and the knowledge to use them, making these some of the earliest sea voyages known anywhere. There was never a continuous land bridge from Asia to Australia. Rising seas after the ice age made the gaps wider, not smaller.

questions.stem: Archaeologists often give dates in 'years BP'. What does BP mean?
options: Before Present, counted back from the year 1950
Before Present, counted back from the year 2000
Before Present, counted back from the day of the dig
Before the Pleistocene, the last great ice age
questions.explanation: BP stands for Before Present, and scientists fixed 'the present' as 1950, around when radiocarbon dating was developed, so that a date does not change depending on when it was measured. So 10,000 BP means about 10,000 years before 1950. Counting from the date of each dig would make the same layer's age shift every year.

questions.stem: An archaeologist wants to date a sand layer about 60,000 years old that holds stone tools but no charcoal or bone. Which method is the best choice?
options: Luminescence dating, which finds when the sand was last in sunlight
Radiocarbon dating, which measures carbon-14 left in the sand grains
Stratigraphy, which gives each layer its exact age in years
Dendrochronology, which counts the yearly growth rings in the layer
questions.explanation: Luminescence dating (thermoluminescence or optically stimulated luminescence) measures energy stored in quartz grains since they were last exposed to sunlight, and it works well beyond 60,000 years. Radiocarbon dating needs organic material such as charcoal or bone, and by about 50,000 years too little carbon-14 is left to measure. Stratigraphy only shows which layers are older or younger; it does not give an age in years.

questions.stem: Mungo Lady and Mungo Man, two of the oldest known human burials in Australia, were found in which World Heritage area?
options: Budj Bim Cultural Landscape
Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park
Willandra Lakes Region
Kakadu National Park
questions.explanation: Lake Mungo is one of the dry lakes of the Willandra Lakes Region in south-western New South Wales, listed as World Heritage in 1981 partly because of these burials. The lakes held fresh water when Mungo Lady and Mungo Man lived there and have since dried out. Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta are in the Northern Territory, and Budj Bim in western Victoria is known for Gunditjmara eel traps.

questions.stem: Mungo Lady's remains, dated to around 40,000 years ago, are significant to world history because they show:
options: the earliest known rock painting made anywhere in Australia
one of the oldest known cremations anywhere in the world
the oldest human skeleton ever found anywhere in the world
that people first reached Australia by travelling down the Murray
questions.explanation: Mungo Lady's body was burned, her bones were broken and burned again, and the remains were buried, making this one of the earliest known cremations in the world and evidence of complex beliefs about death. Much older human remains have been found in Africa, so she is not the oldest skeleton in the world. Mungo Man, found nearby, was buried with his body sprinkled with red ochre.

questions.stem: In 2017 Mungo Man was returned from the Australian National University in Canberra to Lake Mungo. Why was this important to the Traditional Owners?
options: Ancestral remains belong on Country, cared for by their descendants
It allowed scientists to begin dating the remains for the first time
It proved for the first time that Mungo Man was an Aboriginal man
Australian law required all ancient remains to be shown in museums
questions.explanation: For the Paakantyi (Barkindji), Ngiyampaa and Mutthi Mutthi peoples, Mungo Man is an ancestor who was taken from Country in 1974, and returning him restored their responsibility to care for him. His remains had been dated by scientists decades earlier. Returning ancestral remains is called repatriation, and the law does not require remains to be displayed.

questions.stem: As the last ice age ended, rising seas flooded the land between Tasmania and the mainland. Which body of water formed?
options: Torres Strait
The Tasman Sea
The Gulf of Carpentaria
Bass Strait
questions.explanation: Rising seas covered the low plain linking Tasmania to Victoria, forming Bass Strait and separating Tasmanian Aboriginal people from the mainland for thousands of years. Torres Strait formed in the same way but in the far north, separating Cape York from New Guinea and leaving the Torres Strait Islands. The Tasman Sea already existed between Australia and New Zealand.

questions.stem: Boonwurrung accounts from around Port Phillip and Nukunu accounts from Spencer Gulf describe the sea flooding land that people once walked on. When did most of the sea-level rise after the last ice age take place?
options: Between about 200 and 100 years ago
Between about 18,000 and 7,000 years ago
Between about 65,000 and 60,000 years ago
Between about 2,000 and 1,000 years ago
questions.explanation: As the ice sheets melted, sea levels rose by more than 100 metres, reaching close to today's level by around 7,000 years ago and drowning coastal plains around Australia. Oral traditions describing this change have therefore been passed on for many hundreds of generations. The period 65,000 to 60,000 years ago is around when people are thought to have reached Sahul, during a time of low seas.

questions.stem: Diprotodon, the largest marsupial that has ever lived, is best described as:
options: a giant flightless bird distantly related to ducks and geese
a meat-eating 'marsupial lion' with slicing cheek teeth
a giant short-faced kangaroo that browsed on tree leaves
a wombat-like plant-eater about the size of a hippopotamus
questions.explanation: Diprotodon was a heavily built plant-eater, distantly related to wombats, that weighed up to about 2.7 tonnes. The flightless bird is Genyornis, the 'marsupial lion' is Thylacoleo and the short-faced kangaroos include Procoptodon. All were Australian megafauna that lived alongside the first people in Sahul.

questions.stem: Scientists still debate why Australia's megafauna died out. Which two explanations are at the centre of this debate?
options: A drying climate, and the impact of human hunting and burning
A meteorite strike, and volcanic eruptions in central Australia
Diseases from European livestock, and land clearing by settlers
Competition from dingoes, and the spread of introduced rabbits
questions.explanation: Many megafauna species had disappeared by around 40,000 years ago, after people had arrived and while the climate was changing, so researchers argue over how much each factor mattered. Dingoes arrived only a few thousand years ago and rabbits in the 1800s, far too late to be responsible. A meteorite explains the dinosaurs' extinction about 66 million years ago, not the megafauna's.

questions.stem: The Budj Bim Cultural Landscape in western Victoria was World Heritage listed in 2019 for:
options: the rock engravings that the Yolngu carved into the sandstone cliffs
the stone fish traps that the Ngemba built across the Barwon River
the ancient burials found in the dry lake beds of the Willandra Lakes region
the channels, weirs and stone traps the Gunditjmara built to farm eels
questions.explanation: For thousands of years the Gunditjmara shaped the lava flows from the Budj Bim volcano into a system of channels, weirs and ponds to trap, store and harvest kooyang (short-finned eels), one of the world's oldest known aquaculture systems. The Ngemba fish traps across the Barwon River are at Brewarrina in New South Wales. The Yolngu are from north-east Arnhem Land.

questions.stem: The Ngemba stone fish traps on the Barwon River at Brewarrina, known as Baiame's Ngunnhu, worked by:
options: damming the whole river with logs to create a permanent lake full of fish
stretching long woven nets right across the river each spring to catch them
using rock walls and pens to guide fish into ponds where they were caught
using channels cut through old lava flows to raise eels in ponds over winter
questions.explanation: According to Ngemba tradition the traps were designed by the ancestral creator Baiame; stone walls form a maze of pens that fish enter when the river is high and cannot leave as the water falls. Different families were responsible for particular pens, and neighbouring groups shared the traps under strict rules. Channels in lava flows describe Budj Bim in Victoria.

questions.stem: Ground-edge axes found in northern Australia are among the oldest known in the world. What makes an axe 'ground-edge'?
options: It was made from crushed ochre pressed and dried into an axe shape
Its cutting edge was smoothed and sharpened by grinding on rough stone
Its cutting edge was formed by knocking small flakes off it with another stone
It was buried in the ground for months to harden the stone head
questions.explanation: A ground-edge axe has its edge shaped by rubbing it against a coarse stone, often with water and sand, giving a stronger, smoother edge; fragments from Madjedbebe and the Kimberley date back tens of thousands of years. Knocking off flakes, called knapping, is how simpler stone tools were made. Many axe heads were also hafted, or fixed to a wooden handle with resin and binding.

questions.stem: In many Aboriginal societies, people and things belong to one of two halves, which helps decide whom a person may marry. What are these halves called?
options: Totems
Clans
Songlines
Moieties
questions.explanation: A moiety is one of two halves into which a society, and often the whole natural world, is divided, and in many groups people must marry someone from the other moiety. A totem is a natural species or feature that links a person or group to ancestral beings, and clans are smaller family groups descended from shared ancestors. Kinship rules like these, including skin names in some regions, set out each person's relationships and responsibilities.

questions.stem: From at least the 1700s until the early 1900s, Macassan sailors from Sulawesi visited the coast of Arnhem Land each year. What did they mainly come to collect?
options: Sandalwood to sell to temple builders in India
Gold dust to sell to the Dutch traders in the port of Batavia
Pearls to sell to the jewellers of Europe
Trepang (sea cucumber) to sell to Chinese markets
questions.explanation: Macassan crews collected and processed trepang on Australian beaches, trading with Yolngu and other coastal peoples for goods such as cloth, metal knives and tobacco; some Yolngu travelled back to Makassar with them. Dried trepang was prized in China as food and medicine. The visits ended in the early 1900s when the government in charge of the Northern Territory stopped issuing licences.

questions.stem: Pearl shell from the Kimberley coast has been found thousands of kilometres away, as far as South Australia. What does this show?
options: Macassan traders carried the shell inland on camels to sell it
One Kimberley group moved to South Australia, carrying its shell
Goods passed along trade networks that crossed much of the continent
Pearl oysters once lived in rivers that flowed through central Australia
questions.explanation: Kimberley pearl shell, valued for ceremony and decoration, moved from group to group along exchange routes that also carried ochre, stone for axes and other goods, often far beyond where it came from. Camels were brought to Australia only in the 1800s, and Macassan contact was limited to the northern coast.

questions.stem: Murujuga, on the Burrup Peninsula and Dampier Archipelago in Western Australia, holds one of the world's largest collections of:
options: ancient human burial sites
underground ochre mines
rock engravings, or petroglyphs
eel-farming channels and weirs
questions.explanation: Murujuga holds more than a million petroglyphs, some thought to be among the oldest rock art in the world, and it was listed as World Heritage in 2025. Eel-farming channels are found at Budj Bim in Victoria. Like the art of Kakadu, Gariwerd (the Grampians) and Koonalda Cave, Murujuga's engravings are a major source of evidence about First Nations history.

questions.stem: Archaeologists at Troy found about nine main settlements built on top of one another, numbered from Troy I at the bottom to Troy IX at the top. What does this numbering show?
options: Troy I is the oldest settlement and Troy IX the most recent
Troy IX is the oldest, because it was the last one dug up
All nine settlements were built and lived in at the same time
Each number shows the century in which that city was destroyed
questions.explanation: By the law of superposition, in undisturbed layers the lowest is the oldest, so Troy I is the earliest settlement and Troy IX, the Greek and Roman city, the most recent. The order in which layers are excavated says nothing about their age. Several layers show signs of destruction by fire or earthquake before the site was rebuilt.

questions.stem: Which list of periods is in the correct order, earliest first?
options: Palaeolithic, Neolithic, Iron Age, Bronze Age
Palaeolithic, Bronze Age, Neolithic, Iron Age
Palaeolithic, Neolithic, Bronze Age, Iron Age
Neolithic, Palaeolithic, Bronze Age, Iron Age
questions.explanation: The Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) was followed by the Neolithic (New Stone Age), when farming began, then the Bronze Age and the Iron Age as people learned to work metals. Bronze came before iron because iron needs higher temperatures and more skill to smelt. These labels were designed for Europe, western Asia and North Africa, so they do not fit every society, including First Nations Australia.

questions.stem: CT scanning is now widely used to study Egyptian mummies. What is its main advantage?
options: It repairs damaged bandages so that the mummy can be put on public display
It shows bones, organs and objects inside without unwrapping the body
It gives the exact year in which the person died
It reveals the person's name by reading their DNA
questions.explanation: A CT scanner combines thousands of X-ray images into a 3D view, so researchers can see a mummy's age, injuries, illnesses and amulets without damaging it. Dates come from methods such as radiocarbon, and DNA can show family links or diseases, as in studies of Tutankhamun's relatives, but it cannot reveal a name.

questions.stem: LiDAR scanning from aircraft has revealed lost cities hidden under thick forest, such as around Angkor in Cambodia. How does LiDAR work?
options: It sends radio waves deep underground from a cart pushed across the site
It photographs the forest from space and removes the trees with editing software
It detects heat still given off by stone buildings that were once used
It fires laser pulses and times their return to map the ground under the trees
questions.explanation: LiDAR (light detection and ranging) sends millions of laser pulses from an aircraft; some pass through gaps in the canopy and bounce off the ground, producing a detailed map of buried roads, walls and canals. Radio waves sent into the ground from a cart describe ground-penetrating radar, a different method used to find features beneath the surface without digging.

questions.stem: In the 1960s the temples of Abu Simbel in Egypt were cut into huge blocks and rebuilt on higher ground. Why?
options: Tourists' feet and hands were wearing away the carvings
Lake Nasser, behind the new Aswan High Dam, would have flooded them
Desert sand was burying them faster than workers could clear it
An earthquake had cracked the cliff that the temples were carved into
questions.explanation: The Aswan High Dam created Lake Nasser, which would have drowned many Nubian monuments, so UNESCO led an international campaign that moved Abu Simbel, carved for Ramesses II, about 65 metres higher. The success of the rescue helped inspire the World Heritage Convention of 1972. Sand had buried the temples centuries earlier, but that was not why they were moved.

questions.stem: What does it mean when a place such as the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang is inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List?
options: It must be closed to all visitors to stop any further damage to it
It is officially declared to be in danger of being destroyed
It is recognised as having outstanding value to all humanity
UNESCO takes over ownership of it from the country it is in
questions.explanation: World Heritage listing recognises 'outstanding universal value', and the country where the site is promises to protect it, sometimes with international help; ownership stays with that country. Sites facing serious threats can also be placed on a separate List of World Heritage in Danger. Other listed ancient sites include the Great Wall and Mohenjo-daro.

questions.stem: The Bamiyan Buddhas in Afghanistan (2001) and temples at Palmyra in Syria (2015) are both examples of ancient heritage that was:
options: flooded by the lake behind a newly built dam
worn away by millions of tourists over many years
deliberately destroyed by armed groups during conflict
moved to museums overseas to keep it safe from the war
questions.explanation: The Taliban blew up the giant Bamiyan Buddha statues in 2001, and the group known as Islamic State destroyed temples at Palmyra in 2015. Both acts aimed to erase heritage the groups rejected, and they showed that even world-famous sites can be lost. Flooding by a dam is what threatened Abu Simbel in the 1960s.

questions.stem: The Parthenon Sculptures, removed from Athens by agents of Lord Elgin in the early 1800s, are at the centre of a long dispute between:
options: Greece, which wants them returned, and the British Museum
Italy and Greece, over which of the two countries built the Parthenon
Turkey, which claims them, and the British Museum
France and Britain, over which of them first found them
questions.explanation: Elgin's agents removed about half of the surviving sculptures while Greece was ruled by the Ottoman Empire, and they have been in the British Museum since 1816. Greece argues they were taken without proper consent and belong with the Parthenon in Athens, while the museum argues they were acquired legally. The dispute is a well-known example of the debate over returning cultural artefacts.

questions.stem: How have many museums changed the way they care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander collections in recent decades?
options: They display sacred objects more widely so more people can learn about them
They have stopped holding any objects made by First Nations peoples at all
They keep every object permanently, since a collection must never be broken up
They work with communities on how objects are cared for, shown or returned
questions.explanation: Museums now consult Traditional Owners about storage, display and access, often keeping secret or sacred objects out of public view and returning ancestral remains and some objects through repatriation programs. Putting sacred objects on wider display goes against cultural protocols. Museums still hold large First Nations collections, but who decides how they are used has shifted towards communities.

questions.stem: The Greek writer Herodotus, who investigated the wars between Greece and Persia in the 400s BCE, is often called:
options: the 'father of medicine'
the 'father of geometry'
the 'father of democracy'
the 'father of history'
questions.explanation: Herodotus called his work 'histories', meaning inquiries, and collected and compared accounts to explain why the Persian Wars happened, which is why he is called the father of history. Hippocrates is called the father of medicine and Euclid the father of geometry. Thucydides, who wrote about the Peloponnesian War soon after, was stricter about checking evidence.

questions.stem: Sima Qian, an official of the Han dynasty around 100 BCE, is important in the history of China because he:
options: wrote the Records of the Grand Historian, covering over 2,000 years
invented paper so that court records could be kept more cheaply
founded the school of thought that became known as Confucianism
ordered the burning of old books that disagreed with the emperor
questions.explanation: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian traces China's past from the legendary Yellow Emperor to his own time, using court archives, older texts and interviews, and became the model for later Chinese histories. Paper is credited to Cai Lun about two centuries later, and the burning of books was ordered by Qin Shi Huang. His work shows that careful history writing also developed outside the Greek tradition.

questions.stem: How did Roman citizenship differ from citizenship in classical Athens?
options: Rome extended it to freed slaves and, over time, to conquered peoples
Rome allowed women citizens to vote in its assemblies and the Senate
Rome required every citizen to have two parents born in the city
Rome gave citizens no voting rights, only the duty of serving in the army
questions.explanation: Athens, after a law of 451 BCE, limited citizenship to people with two Athenian parents and rarely granted it to outsiders. Rome gave citizenship to slaves freed by citizen owners and gradually to allies and provinces, until in 212 CE almost all free people in the empire became citizens. Women could not vote in either society.

questions.stem: The motives of European explorers in the 1400s and 1500s are often summed up as 'God, gold and glory'. What does 'God' refer to?
options: Carrying Christian pilgrims by sea to Jerusalem
Spreading Christianity to the peoples they met
Escaping religious persecution at home in Europe
Proving to the Church that the world was round
questions.explanation: Explorers and the rulers who paid for their voyages aimed to convert other peoples to Christianity, and missionaries sailed with many expeditions; 'gold' meant wealth and 'glory' fame for themselves and their countries. Escaping persecution motivated some later settlers, such as English Puritans in North America in the 1600s. Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round.

questions.stem: In the 1400s, why did European merchants and rulers want to find a sea route to Asia?
options: Spices reached Europe overland through many middlemen, so they were very costly
Chinese emperors had banned silk and spices from being sold to Europe
European ships were not allowed to sail on the Mediterranean Sea
Asian traders refused to accept gold or silver in payment for goods
questions.explanation: Pepper, cloves and nutmeg passed through many hands, including Ottoman, Arab and Venetian merchants, before reaching Europe, and each added to the price. After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, a sea route that cut out these middlemen looked even more attractive to Portugal and Spain. Asian traders in fact wanted silver and gold, as Europe had few goods they needed.

questions.stem: Which instrument let sailors work out their latitude by measuring the height of the Sun or a star above the horizon?
options: The caravel
The marine chronometer
The astrolabe
The magnetic compass
questions.explanation: The mariner's astrolabe measured the angle of the Sun or Pole Star above the horizon, from which a navigator could calculate how far north or south they were. A compass shows direction but not position, and the caravel was a small, fast ship. The marine chronometer, which solved the problem of longitude, was not developed until the 1700s.

questions.stem: Which explorer became the first European to reach India by sailing around Africa, in 1498?
options: Bartolomeu Dias
Christopher Columbus
Ferdinand Magellan
Vasco da Gama
questions.explanation: Vasco da Gama sailed from Portugal around the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut in India in 1498, opening a direct sea route for the spice trade. Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the Cape ten years earlier, in 1488, but turned back before reaching India. Columbus sailed west in 1492 hoping to reach Asia and arrived in the Caribbean instead.

questions.stem: The expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan from 1519 to 1522 was the first to sail around the world. Who completed the voyage?
options: Juan Sebastián Elcano, after Magellan was killed in the Philippines
Magellan himself, who returned to Spain in triumph in 1522
Francis Drake, who took command when Magellan fell ill
Vasco da Gama, who joined the fleet at the Spice Islands
questions.explanation: Magellan was killed at Mactan in the Philippines in 1521, and Elcano commanded the one surviving ship, the Victoria, back to Spain in 1522 with only a small fraction of the crew that had set out. Francis Drake made England's first circumnavigation decades later, from 1577 to 1580.

questions.stem: Which European made the first recorded landing on the Australian coast, on Cape York Peninsula in 1606?
options: Abel Tasman, in the Heemskerck
James Cook, in the Endeavour
Willem Janszoon, in the Duyfken
Dirk Hartog, in the Eendracht
questions.explanation: Willem Janszoon, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, charted part of western Cape York in 1606, and his crew clashed with local Aboriginal people. Dirk Hartog landed on an island off Western Australia in 1616, Abel Tasman reached Tasmania in 1642, and Cook charted the east coast in 1770.

questions.stem: In 1770 James Cook charted the east coast of Australia. Where did he claim the coast for Britain?
options: Kamay Botany Bay, where he first came ashore
Sydney Cove, where the First Fleet later settled
Port Phillip, on the southern coast of the continent
Possession Island, near the tip of Cape York
questions.explanation: Cook first landed at Kamay Botany Bay in April 1770, where Gweagal men opposed the landing, but he made his claim to the whole east coast on Possession Island in Torres Strait in August 1770, without the consent of the First Nations peoples living there. Sydney Cove was settled in 1788 under Arthur Phillip, and Cook never entered Port Phillip.

questions.stem: In 1493 Pope Alexander VI issued a papal bull, Inter caetera, that became part of the Doctrine of Discovery. What did the Doctrine claim?
options: Explorers had to stay away from any lands that people already lived on
Christian rulers could claim lands not already ruled by Christians
Indigenous peoples owned their lands and had to be paid for them
Lands found by explorers had to be shared by all European kingdoms
questions.explanation: The Doctrine of Discovery held that a Christian nation that 'discovered' land not ruled by Christians could claim it, ignoring the rights of the peoples living there. Inter caetera granted Spain lands west of a line in the Atlantic, which led to the Treaty of Tordesillas the next year. European powers used these ideas to justify taking land across the Americas, Africa, Asia and the Pacific.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Tordesillas, signed in 1494, is significant because it:
options: divided newly found lands between Spain and Portugal along a line in the Atlantic
ended the long wars that Spain and England fought over their colonies in the Americas
gave the Netherlands sole rights to trade in the Spice Islands of Asia
divided up the continent of Africa among all the major European powers
questions.explanation: The treaty set a line about 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: Spain could claim lands to the west and Portugal lands to the east, which is why Brazil became Portuguese. No one asked the peoples living in those lands, and other powers such as England and France ignored it. The division of Africa came much later, at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85.

questions.stem: Why is the Doctrine of Discovery still debated by Indigenous peoples, governments and churches today?
options: It is still the law that decides all First Nations land claims in Australia today
It promised Indigenous peoples a share of profits from their land, never paid
It was the treaty that ended the wars between settlers and Native Americans
It was used as a legal basis for taking Indigenous land, including in US courts
questions.explanation: In 1823 the United States Supreme Court relied on the Doctrine of Discovery in Johnson v. M'Intosh, ruling that Native Americans held only a right to occupy their land, and the idea shaped land law in other settler colonies. In Australia the High Court's Mabo decision of 1992 rejected terra nullius and recognised native title. In 2023 the Vatican formally repudiated the Doctrine.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) was signed by representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs. Why has it been disputed ever since?
options: It handed New Zealand to France rather than to Britain
It was signed after the New Zealand Wars, as a peace settlement
The English and Māori versions differ on whether chiefs gave up sovereignty
Māori chiefs refused to sign it, so it never came into force at all
questions.explanation: In the English text the chiefs ceded sovereignty to the Crown, but the Māori text, which most chiefs signed, used a word closer to 'governance' and promised them continued chieftainship over their lands and treasures. Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars from the 1840s to the 1870s, after the treaty was signed. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated breaches of the treaty.

questions.stem: From 1757 China's Qing government allowed European traders to do business only at Canton (Guangzhou), and only through licensed Chinese merchants. What does this show?
options: China welcomed European traders into every one of its ports
China had banned all trade with foreigners completely
China controlled its contact with Europeans on its own terms
China had already been colonised by Britain and France
questions.explanation: Under the Canton system the Qing limited where Europeans could go, whom they could trade with and when, while Europeans paid in silver for tea, silk and porcelain. China was not colonised; Britain later used the First Opium War (1839–1842) to force open more ports. Indigenous and Asian responses to European contact ranged from resistance and negotiation to controlled trade like this.

questions.stem: Historians use the term 'Columbian Exchange' for what happened after 1492. What does it refer to?
options: The transfer of crops, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world
The first trade agreement that Columbus signed with the Taíno people of the Caribbean islands
The exchange of land between Spain and Portugal set out in a treaty of 1494
The swap of prisoners between Spain and the Aztecs after the conquest of Mexico
questions.explanation: After 1492, maize, potatoes and tomatoes spread from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia, while horses, cattle, wheat and sugar went the other way. Diseases such as smallpox, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity, killed a very large share of the population. The 1494 land division was the Treaty of Tordesillas, a separate event.
